reader_question: How often has the Senate voted on ending debate, Congress by Congress?
grade_line: Documented: the Senate’s own count of cloture votes
title: The Senate held 298 votes on ending debate in the Congress of 2019 and 2020, after no more than seven in any Congress before 1971.
reading_guide: Each circle is one two-year Congress, placed at its first year, and its area is the number of votes on ending debate. Where circles overlap, every outline still shows; a short tick marks a Congress with none.
measure_line: Senate votes on cloture, a motion to end debate, on bills and nominations together, by Congress, from the 65th Congress (1917 and 1918), the first under the Senate’s cloture rule, to the 119th Congress to date, United States Senate.
notes: Until 1975, ending debate took two-thirds of senators voting. Since then it takes three-fifths of all senators for most matters, and changes in 2013 and 2017 lowered it to a simple majority for nominations.
The counts mix bills and nominations.
The 119th Congress, 2025 and 2026, is still in session; its 294 votes so far are drawn with a dashed outline.
alt: Bubble timeline of Senate votes on ending debate in each Congress from 1917 to 2026. The circles stay tiny or absent until about 1970, grow through the 1970s to 2000s, and swell after 2007; the largest is 298 votes in the Congress of 2019 and 2020, and the current Congress has held 294 so far.

notes_internal: Maker B, round 1. Data plan row 27, rule 14.41. Domain D04 from the sidecar; no state named.

Checked by script against senate-cloture-motions-by-congress.csv: 55 Congresses; the most votes on cloture 298 in the 116th (2019); no Congress before the 92nd (1971) held more than 7 (the 69th and 89th); 11 Congresses held none; the 119th, still in session, 294.

Rule history in note 1 comes from the sidecar's qualification and printed line; its 2013 and 2017 changes are on the sidecar's 'unconfirmed' list (not read on a Senate page on November 11), which the research lead may confirm.

H09: the window starts with the first Congress under the cloture rule and runs to today; Congresses are two-year terms, so no period splits at an inauguration. Read from the left and the right: the title counts votes and names no party or leader.
